articles.title: Budget 2026: The two big calls Chancellor John Healey has to make
articles.summary: He must consider the longevity of Iran war economic pressures and how to sustain modest optimism, writes the BBC's Faisal Islam.
articles.body:
"It is tough," John Healey admitted to me earlier this month when I asked him if there had been too much doom-mongering?

"Conflicts, uncertainty, driving up inflation, driving up interest rates. But we've got great strengths. We've got good reasons to be confident about the future of Britain," he insisted.

The new scheme to try and help young people get on the property ladder, announced on Saturday, was aimed at boosting confidence in the economy.

But the chancellor is now facing two big decisions before his inaugural Budget on 28 October.

Firstly, about the longevity of the economic pressures caused by the Iran War, and then about how to sustain a modest but notable uptick in economic spirits, through yet more global turbulence.

In his first weeks as chancellor the oil price fell as low as $75 a barrel while the yield - the effective interest rate - on 10-year government bonds was 4.9%.

Just over two months later oil has largely traded above $100 and the 10-year yield is at around 5.4%. It is the ultimate double whammy for a chancellor facing his first Budget.

Yet there is something unusual about this energy shock. It could quickly reverse, as illustrated earlier in the summer when assumptions about a deescalation in the US Iran conflict led to sharp falls in energy prices and yields.

In New York this week both President Trump and his Iranian counterpart President Pezeshkian suggested November's US midterm elections were connected to when the war might end.

The Iranians would wait until after the elections to seek peace because the war's impact on the cost of living - particularly soaring diesel costs - could damage him electorally, the US president told the UN General Assembly.

The Iranian president said his nation "didn't want it to get to the midterms".

Both sides in this war are feeling the economic squeeze of conflict.

The 3 November vote is six days after the Budget. No one could rely on there being a settlement by then, but it is plausible.

So the Budget tax, spend and borrowing forecasts could be based on a prolonged conflict, which is actually on the cusp of ending, or even already ended.

The chancellor has to therefore decide whether to plan for the worst, and make some painful permanent tax and spend decisions, or buy some time.

One option is to let borrowing take some of the strain, by tolerating a reduction in the £24bn of headroom - room for manoeuvre against its self-imposed borrowing rules - left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves.

This year's headroom will be judged in three years rather than four, so there is some rationale as to why a smaller number over a closer target might be appropriate.

And while higher inflation means higher interest costs, it also means higher cash tax receipts, at a time when thresholds continue to be frozen.

There is a second consideration. The hopeful optimism "vibes" strategy of the Burnham administration appears to have had some impact.

The longest running UK consumer confidence survey has hit a two-year high. Among younger people it has not been this high since before Brexit.

Some data companies call it a "Burnham bounce", although the weather and World Cup were also factors.

There is evidence, more mixed, that business optimism has also perked up in recent months, possibly because of earlier falls in energy prices, though this has been clouded by anticipation of possible tax rises. Business group, the Institute of Directors said this was despite, rather than because of, the new government.

While no one should get too carried away with these turnarounds, they do stand in contrast to the admitted mistake of the Starmer government in talking up consumer pain, two years ago.

The question for the chancellor is whether better consumer and business spirits can be reconciled with the need for a "challenging" Budget?

Indeed, it's important to determine how much of the summer global bond market shock is solely down to the impact of the Iran war and how much is more structural.

Governments are facing new and intense competition in bond markets from the world's biggest AI businesses. In addition, the UK has had recent, prominent political and economic uncertainty.

Right now the bond markets are like a pack of wolves stalking red deer, probing for weaknesses.

"At times like this you don't want to be at the back of the herd," said one very senior former Treasury adviser.

UK and US warned to take action on spiralling debt costs by IMF

Unexpected UK borrowing surge adds to pre-Budget pressure on chancellor

Government borrowing, bonds and yields explained

In response, the Treasury has pointed to the UK having the highest growth and the fastest falling borrowing of the major G7 countries so far this year and our overall energy prices starting to decouple from high and volatile gas prices.

However, the IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva this week dismissed the idea that advanced nations could pause their fiscal homework, while the Gulf situation calmed.

"Bring debt levels down, make fiscal consolidation as a priority… it is impossible to stress strongly enough how critical it is to get the courage to take the steps that are necessary," Georgieva told me, acknowledging the UK's "fairly consistent, credible" plans.

Then there is the curious conundrum of British productivity. Last year, the government's official forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) downgraded the UK's productivity peformance, leading to a notable hit to the public finances.

Now the UK's productivity record has been upgraded materially by the Office for National Statistics, although this is because of fewer hours worked. There could therefore be an argument to reverse some of that downgrade.

Separately, the new chair of the OBR Jonathan Haskel is known for his argument that official statistics understate investment in intangibles like software and data. His latest research suggests AI-related investment is already visible in US productivity figures, and he has long been optimistic about tech's impact on the future.

While it seems unlikely that such factors will make it into the OBR's calculations next month, there is a real debate here.

Officially, however, part of the job at the Budget is to identify cuts to fund the Defence Investment Plan, inherited from Sir Keir. That's before funding the additional move to 3% of GDP and a new social care system.

Even a promise of less welfare spending looks like being built on an upfront investment in jobs for young people.

One change from last year is that so far, the government has parked the "pitch-rolling" with a silence that would rival the Trappist monks.

Instead, policy announcements are strategically timed such as the "Your First Home" scheme just as the Labour party conference got underway. We can expect to hear plenty more as the Budget nears.

articles.title: Who is in Celebrity Traitors? From Michael Sheen to Maya Jama
articles.summary: The reality TV game show returns on Thursday, with 21 stars vying to win £100,000 for their chosen charity.
articles.body:
Celebrity Traitors returns next week for a second round of deception and amateur detective work.

Hosted by Claudia Winkleman, the Traitors castle will welcome 21 new celebrities on Thursday, as a group of famous "faithfuls" attempts to work out which among them are - and perhaps, always have been - "traitors", secretly murdering contestants each night.

Last year's show provided Bafta's most memorable TV moment - an award voted for by the British public - when traitor Alan Carr broke down in tears at the end of the final having bluffed his way to a win by hiding in plain sight.

Let's have a stab in the dark, then, at who might follow in Jonathan Ross's footsteps as this year's "big dog", and who, like singer Cat Burns, could fly under the radar?

If Carr was the star of last year's show, then perhaps his fellow TV funnymen could be the ones to watch this time around.

Naturally good readers of a room and skilled at misdirection, comedians can inject some comic relief into those tense roundtable moments.

It worked for Carr, who was considered to be less of a threat and more out of his depth by the other sleuths.

This time around, stand-up star Joe Lycett , 38, is one of the leading candidates for the role of class clown. Known for his quick wit and political stunts, Lycett told the BBC he asked Carr for advice on "how to spot a rotten little traitor like you".

Last year's winner replied: "Just anyone that's sweating and giggling."

With his brightly coloured outfits, Lycett will bring some glamour to the castle, if and when he's not donning the famous dark cloak.

"There's a lot of variety and silly stuff that I might not get to wear at all if I end up doing a Paloma," he noted, with reference to Paloma Faith, who was brutally killed off early doors last year by her supposed friend, Carr.

If laughing all the way to the winning line is to work again, then it's hard to look beyond James Acaster .

Anyone who has seen his Netflix special Repertoire or heard his podcast Off Menu will know his deadpan, absurdist humour and whimsical flights of fancy could make it difficult to tell whether he is telling the truth or not.

A "huge fan" of the show since the first non-celebrity edition in 2022, Acaster, 41, said he would prefer to be a faithful as he wasn't good at lying - though Carr did previously say something similar...

Romesh Ranganathan 's dry humour and wry presenting style saw him succeed Anne Robinson as the host of The Weakest Link revival in 2021. Could it help him to become a more believable traitor or faithful?

The former maths teacher and now comedy podcaster, 48, blamed his youngest son, who was "desperate for me to come on", for his reluctant participation this year.

One of his best friends on the comedy circuit, Parenting Hell podcaster Rob Beckett , is another of this year's funniest contestants.

A decade's worth of friendship with the 8 Out of 10 Cats and Mock the Week panellist could count for nothing in the castle, Ranganathan said. He believes Beckett, 40, is "just as easily going to be on my side as he is going to twist the knife in my back given the opportunity".

One of the nation's other most celebrated comics, Miranda Hart will no doubt be a big personality among the group.

In her self-titled sitcom, she starred as an awkward, accident-prone shopkeeper. Her apparent clumsiness and warm, self-deprecating persona might make her seem more trustworthy (rightly or wrongly).

After a spell of ill-health, Hart, 53, hopes "the joy of mucking about on television again will hopefully outweigh some of the challenges".

Irish comedian Joanne McNally , 43, could also be the joker of the pack this year. Her popular podcast My Therapist Ghosted Me is full of gossip, oversharing and comic bickering - music to the ears of the Traitors producers, no doubt.

Her stand-up is confessional and brutally honest. But honesty gets you nowhere in this game - or does it?

The "Big Dog Theory" was a piece of gameplay logic proposed by ex-rugby union star Joe Marler during roundtable discussions last year.

His reasoning was that one of the most famous contestants, AKA the big dogs, would have been chosen as a traitor to cause mass confusion (and, presumably, strong viewing figures).

Marler wondered out loud whether the big dog traitor in question was Sir Stephen Fry (no) or Jonathan Ross (yes).

For the new series, a glut of huge names and personalities from across the worlds of film, TV, music, modelling and broadcasting have also been selected.

Michael Sheen, the award-winning Welsh actor and campaigner, is perhaps the biggest dog in the fight, so will come under real scrutiny.

Sheen, 57, is acclaimed for his ability to convincingly portray a range of different personalities on screen, from Tony Blair to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor via Brian Clough.

But in real life, he's seen more as a loveable golden retriever than a Rottweiler, despite his success. Which version of him we shall see on the show remains to be seen.

Fellow big screen charmer Richard E. Grant , 69, who starred in films such as Withnail and I, may also leave some of the less well-known celebrities star-struck at first, as might American-British supermodel/actress Jerry Hall.

Hall, 70, shares four children with ex-partner Mick Jagger and has also been married to media mogul Rupert Murdoch.

Love Island presenter Maya Jama , 32, and University Challenge host, journalist and YouTuber Amol Rajan are also powerhouses in the world of broadcasting.

Speaking ahead of the show, 43-year-old Rajan, who is in it to win it, said : "I don't want to go in there and at round table number one be Mr Forensic Investigator!

"However, I do interview politicians for a living, and I really have to pursue answers to questions."

He's conscious of putting "a target" on his back too soon, so plans to form alliances.

"To begin with, I want to try and make friends and keep my head down," he added.

EastEnders hardman turned hard-hitting documentarian Ross Kemp , 62, might prove popular once the tasks get physical.

And we don't know yet whether to expect the soppy You're Beautiful balladeer James Blunt , 52, or the prolific (and hilarious) online troll of the same name.

Either way, if the Big Dog Theory holds true, then one of the above will surely find themselves in the traitors' turret before long.

Little Mix and solo singing star Leigh-Anne Pinnock , 34, may be a big dog in the world of pop music, but she comes across as a down-to-earth family woman these days.

Don't be fooled, though, as she has a wealth of experience of managing relationships under intense public pressure from her girl group days.

Meanwhile, another potential dark horse, Bella Ramsey , revealed they had been playing a version of The Traitors since they were 10 years old, even hosting events at home - so should be well-prepared.

Now 22, the Last of Us star, who also featured in Game of Thrones, is the youngest of this year's contestants but should not be underestimated. The Traitors castle should be a cakewalk compared with the apocalypse or the Battle of Winterfell, right?

The plan is to be "instinctive, measured, and perceptive", Ramsey said. "I will be keeping my opinions to myself until I feel it's absolutely the right time to share them."

King Kenny , a member of popular British YouTube collective Beta Squad, is known for pranks, vlogs and more recently (and briefly), boxing.

The 29-year-old will be hoping the class of 2026 has more faith in online influencers than last year, when his Beta Squadmate Niko Omilana was the first player banished from the castle.

Omilana's early exit also sparked a discussion among some critics about non-white contestants being voted off UK/US reality game shows at an early stage, and whether unconscious bias may play a role.

Mathematician and broadcaster, Hannah Fry , who co-hosts The Rest is Science podcast, could fill David Olusoga's intellectual shoes this year.

Historian Olusoga quietly made it to the final last year despite having repeatedly voted out faithfuls thinking they were traitors.

Fry, 42, said she was "here to fulfil the nerd quota" and was taking the responsibility "extremely seriously".

She added: "I would say people tend to think I'm smarter than I actually am, bluntly, and I don't think that's going to serve me particularly well as I may be seen as a bit of a threat."

If the comedians are aiming to be the next Carr, then who could be the new Cat Burns and fly under the radar all the way to the final?

US actress Myha'la , 30, who plays Harper Stern in banking bonkbuster series Industry, may be top pick.

Unlike her ruthless character on the show, she said she was more of a "kill them with kindness kind of girl rather than a blatantly bullish bulldog". She added: "All that said, I want to be a Traitor. Obviously!"

She's deliberately planned her look - clothes, hair and jewellery - to separate herself from Stern and "be seen as me and not that character".

Julie Hesmondhalgh , will be known to audiences Up North especially as Roy Cropper's wife Hayley in the soap Coronation Street, between 1998 and 2014.

articles.title: Hanle:  The young women guiding tourists through India's night sky
articles.summary: Astronomy tourism is giving young women in Hanle income, confidence and a new role in their community.
articles.body:
Strong winds sweep across this remote village in India's Himalayan Ladakh region, but no one seems to mind. Dinner is over, yet, instead of bed, many people are gathering outside.

At 14,764ft (4,500m) above sea level, Hanle is known for its exceptionally clear, dark skies . Wrapped in thick jackets, woollen caps and gloves, tourists and visitors gather to see the Milky Way and look through telescopes at planets, the Moon and distant stars.

Among them are four young women: Palzes Angmo, Tsering Dolker, Tsering Yangdol and Padma Chamchot.

They are Hanle's astro-ambassadors, trained to guide visitors through the night sky.

By day, they cook meals, clean rooms and look after guests at their family-run homestays. By night, they set up telescopes, trace constellations with laser pointers and explain what visitors are seeing in the dark skies.

These women - all in their late 20s - grew up watching these stars, but it was only a few years ago that they learnt to study them through a telescope.

"The sky here has always been twinkling like this," 28-year-old Dolker says.

The difference today is that people travel hundreds of kilometres to see what locals have long regarded as an ordinary part of life.

Hanle's remote, high-altitude location, dry air and lack of light pollution make its skies prized by astronomers. The cold desert offers suitable observing conditions on around 260 nights a year.

Hanle is also home to the Indian Astronomical Observatory, run by the Indian Institute of Astrophysics, and is a major centre for astronomical research. In 2022, it became India's first Dark Sky Reserve, helping protect its pristine skies from artificial light and putting Hanle on the astronomy tourism map.

Visitor numbers have since surged: from about 3,000 a year five years ago to nearly 30,000 in 2024-25, according to government figures.

As visitors grew, so did opportunities for locals.

In 2022, the Ladakh administration and Indian Institute of Astrophysics trained 24 young people from Hanle and nearby villages in astronomy. These four women were among them.

Over 15 days, they learnt to identify stars, planets and constellations, navigate the night sky, operate telescopes and photograph the Milky Way on their phones.

Becoming astronomy guides was never part of their plans. They were nervous when they first handled the equipment, fearing they might break something. Gradually, they learnt how it worked and grew confident using it.

Four years on, they are confident astronomers, with evenings beginning around 9pm.

They position telescopes for the night's planets and constellations before guiding visitors from local homestays.

They show them the Moon's craters, Saturn's rings, Vega - the brightest star in the night sky - and other planets, using laser pointers to trace constellations and objects visible to the naked eye.

Then comes the Milky Way. At 11pm each night, the village switches off its lights, plunging Hanle into darkness as visitors scramble to photograph the now-brilliant galaxy.

"When people look through the telescope and capture a photo alongside the Milky Way, they experience immense joy. We also help them with their mobile phone settings so they can capture the Milky Way," Padma Chamchot says.

It often starts with helping one visitor take a picture and ends with a long queue. The women take pictures for their own social media too, comparing notes on the stars and other sights they captured that night.

Hanle has few hotels and no resorts, so visitors mostly stay in family-run homestays, often extensions of their homes. Chamchot's family runs one too.

"Taking care of guests, cooking meals, cleaning rooms, and managing household chores fills our day," she says.

"From nine in the evening, we begin setting up the telescopes for the night's stargazing sessions."

Their families' homestays remain the main income source, but the women earn about 25,000 rupees ($260; £193) a month from astronomy, charging 200 rupees a session. Income dips during the harsh winter, when few tourists visit, but the earnings have given them greater financial independence: they no longer need to ask their parents for money.

"We can save our earnings and spend them on things we want - including new phones," Padma says.

For the astro-ambassadors, the transformation has been personal as much as financial.

"Before taking on this work, we lacked confidence," they say.

However, the growing popularity of Hanle comes with risks. The same tourism that supports local livelihoods could also threaten the darkness that makes Hanle unique.

Visitor numbers have surged, fuelled partly by social media posts about Hanle's night skies and its location on the route to Umling La, which is among the world's highest motorable mountain passes. But more tourists also mean more traffic, construction and artificial light - all threats to the darkness they come to see.

Sonam Jorphail, a senior engineer and head of outreach at the IAO, says tourism is creating jobs and driving development in Hanle, but growth must be managed to protect its dark skies.

"They bridge the gap between the science community and common people - locals and visitors," Jorphail adds.

But longtime residents say Hanle's night sky is already changing. Padma's father, Dhuntup Chamchot, in his 70s, remembers when the skies were even darker.

"Back then, when the weather was good, people would often sleep outdoors under the open sky," he says.

The young women often take their families stargazing too.

"We frequently show the night sky to our families through the telescope. They enjoy looking at it now," says Yangdol, one of the astro-ambassadors. "If one of us takes even a single day off, the families ask why the telescope was not set up," she jokes.

The women say they have no desire to leave Hanle or its dark skies. They hope for advanced training and better telescopes and eyepieces to enhance visitors' experience.

Four years ago, the equipment was unfamiliar; now, they are building a future around the stars.

articles.title: Can you be healthy if you eat ultra-processed foods? I asked a dietitian
articles.summary: UPFs are linked to a range of health problems. But no-one seems to be able to agree why.
articles.body:
Going to the supermarket has become a minefield.

I'm in aisle 15, reading long lists of ingredients and worrying if what's in my trolley is good for me or not.

There's growing evidence that a hefty proportion of the food we consume could be damaging to our health, with ultra-processed foods (UPFs) linked to a range of health problems.

But I've had enough of second-guessing myself and panicking I'm poisoning my child if I feed him chicken nuggets, so I've given my shopping list to a dietitian to analyse.

It depends who you ask. A basic rule of thumb is that to be ultra-processed a product needs more than five ingredients, with at least one not normally found in your kitchen - things like emulsifiers, additives and flavourings.

There is a large and growing body of evidence that shows UPFs are linked to obesity, cardiovascular disease and metabolic disorders such as diabetes, as well as mental health problems and even premature death.

But scientists, doctors and dietitians can't agree on why. Is it purely down to the high fat, sugar, salt and calorie content? Or is the ultra-processing also a factor?

Studies show more than half the calories we consume in the UK come from ultra-processed food . Dr Chris van Tulleken has written books and made documentaries about how bad these foods can be, and he tells me they're "almost impossible to avoid" - even his own family's diet includes a few.

And my shopping list isn't UPF-free either.

Maeve Hanan, a member of the British Dietetic Association, pauses as she scans through some of my weekly shopping list (there was more fruit and veg, honest) and points to a box of bran flakes.

"This is ultra-processed, but I often buy this for my family. It's got so many health benefits."

Hanan says there's a "growing hysteria" about UPFs.

"Mainly because the messaging around them is so black and white," she says. "This food is good. This food is bad.

"It just fuels fear - and fear around food is never good."

So what is her verdict on my grocery shopping?

Not as bad as I expected, I'm relieved to learn. While there are UPFs in there, that doesn't necessarily make it an unhealthy food shop. In fact, Hanan says, "there's a good mix of foods which cover each food group".

Just because some products have a long ingredient list, it doesn't make them "inherently bad", she explains, with the nutritional value "far more important".

What about foods that contain ingredients I can barely pronounce, never mind recognise? Hanan takes my son's chicken nuggets as an example.

"There are mandatory vitamins and minerals which manufacturers in the UK are required to add to white wheat flour such as calcium carbonate, niacin and thiamin," she says.

Raising agents, such as disodium diphosphate, are used alongside sodium bicarbonate (baking powder) to make the batter crisp and light.

Hanan says even the most chemical-sounding ingredients will have been tested and approved under UK food laws.

"But while chicken nuggets are a good source of protein," she warns, "they are higher in fat and salt than a plain chicken breast, so I would eat them in moderation as part of a balanced diet."

I tell Hanan my son usually eats them with raw carrot sticks and pasta.

"One food does not make your diet healthy or unhealthy," she says, "it's about getting that balance over time."

Megan Bamford believes cutting out UPFs from her diet has helped her manage irritable bowel syndrome and chronic pain.

But now, as a mum to two young children, cooking from scratch is not always viable. Her eldest, seven-year-old Ella, has struggled on and off with food since she was little.

"It's not always easy to feed your children what you think they should eat," Megan says. "Ella has been poorly in the past because of her severe picky eating - we had no choice but to give her ultra-processed food from a packet."

So Megan's kitchen is still full of fruit, vegetables, seeds and oats but there are now also breakfast cereals, crisps, biscuits and other processed foods too.

She looks for food with five ingredients or fewer.

"Most of the snacks, pizzas, and cereal I buy are not ultra-processed," she says. "I'm happy with that. I feed my children in the best way I can, I choose the healthiest options I can find."

Struggling to focus? What you eat might be affecting your brain

While many UPFs are high in fat, sugar and salt, which we know cause a whole range of health problems, some scientists say there is not as much understanding about what the act of processing does to our food.

Author and food scientist Prof David Julian McClements says the "ultra-processed food idea is not very well defined".

"Focussing on the processing element is a bit of red herring," he says, "I don't think that's the main problem here."

Some studies suggest the more processed food is, the easier it is to overeat it. Others link UPFs to changes in our gut microbiome. But McClements says there is no conclusive evidence to say this alone inherently damages our health.

But given he works in the food industry, does he have a vested interest?

"Any successful food scientist works a lot with the food industry," McClements says, "and I think trying to get rid of UPFs is holding back innovation."

So many of us lead busy lives, he says, convenience is a major part of society.

"What I want to do is to redesign processed foods to make them healthier," he says.

When I put this to van Tulleken he pauses for breath. He's just been highlighting the high sugar content in various breakfast cereals while waving an empty box of a very sugary and chocolatey one at me. I feel a pang of guilt, knowing my seven-year-old son can get through several bowls in a single sitting.

"UPFs are tasty, they are moreish - that's the whole point," van Tulleken says. "Of course, we can make UPFs healthier - but then they're not as nice.

"The food companies know very well how to make healthy food. The reason they don't is because it's not profitable."

He says there's growing evidence which shows industrial processing does affect our health and that businesses control the food market in a way that is "very harmful".

"What we need for starters is better food labelling so we know which foods have high fat, sugar and salt content which we know is bad for us - and that makes up the majority of UPFs."

The Food and Drink Federation, which represents food and drink manufacturers in the UK, strongly disagrees with van Tulleken's claims. It says it has invested millions of pounds "in healthier product innovation" and its members have "cut the salt, sugar and calories from their products by almost a fifth just in the last five years".

"This work," it says, "has been done in line with government regulation and dietary guidance, which focusses on the nutritional content of food rather than the level of processing."

So as I slide four chicken nuggets on to my son's dinner plate - alongside his carrots and pasta - I'm not feeling the usual shame and panic. He's an active little boy, he doesn't have nuggets every night, and he's eaten from a range of food groups through the day.

He gives me a grin. "This is the best tea ever, Mummy," he says.

One day I'm sure he will eat less beige food, but, for now, he's healthy (I hope) and happy.

articles.title: Time running out for Tennessee killer Christa Pike who says she's too damaged for death row
articles.summary: Lawyers for Pike, who killed a fellow student in 1995, say she should get clemency and would not be sentenced to death if the crime happened today.
articles.body:
Ashlee Sellars last heard from her friend Christa Pike earlier this week, when Pike texted her from her cell on death row as she prepares to be killed by lethal injection by the US state of Tennessee.

Pike told Sellars she does not want any of her loved ones to be present on Wednesday when she is executed.

"She doesn't want us to experience that," Sellars says.

Sellars finds it hard to reconcile this woman, whom she has only known to be kind and protective, with the person who committed a heinous crime 31 years ago.

Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend at the time, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens.

The murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995 when Colleen was found with a pentagram, a symbol of Satanic ritual, carved into her chest.

Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull.

A year later she was sentenced to death, while Shipp - who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole.

Now, after years of failed appeals, Pike's execution has been set for Wednesday. If it goes ahead, she will be the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Only 18 women have been executed in the US since the 1970s, compared to 1,663 men.

Colleen's mother has said she wants Pike's execution to happen so that her daughter "finally can be resting".

But Pike's lawyers, who filed a 226-page clemency petition, are still hoping for a last-minute reprieve, and UN human rights experts have also called for the execution to be stopped.

Pike has a documented history of childhood sexual abuse, abandonment and neglect. Her lawyers believe that if she was found guilty of the same crime today as a teenager she would not receive a death sentence.

In the years since her sentencing, her defence team have uncovered details about her childhood that they say the jury never had the chance to consider.

"It is mind-boggling that they did not present any of her history of abuse and rape, even though they knew about it," says Sandra Babcock, an expert in gender and the death penalty at Cornell Law School, who has worked on Pike's defence.

"Her case is so uniquely compelling, not just because of her really incomprehensible history of sexual violence but the combination of that with her youth and her mental illness."

In 1995, forensic psychologist Dr Diana McCoy was hired by Pike's defence team and found she was severely neglected by both of her parents. McCoy's report found Pike was physically and sexually abused by several of her mother's husbands and boyfriends, and raped several times, once when she was 11 and again aged 17. Later it was discovered that she was repeatedly raped as a toddler by her grandmother's boyfriend. McCoy said Pike's mother didn't believe her that these rapes happened.

But Pike's trial lawyer did not put McCoy on the stand or call many of the witnesses she recommended. These details emerged more than a decade later in a court hearing reviewing her case, when a new team of lawyers claimed ineffective assistance of counsel, a claim that was denied by the judge.

In 2021 Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder in prison and has been medicated since.

Later, another forensic psychologist working for Pike's defence, Dr Bethany Brand, who assessed Pike in 2023, said her case was extremely rare because she was abused by so many people who should have protected her.

"Her childhood was replete with physical, sexual, and emotional abuse. She was sexually violated by a number of men, starting before she was school age," she says.

Brand says Pike had untreated manic episodes due to bipolar disorder and untreated PTSD. "Both of those things together absolutely influenced how threatened she felt by the girl she ended up killing and her lack of emotional control in that situation."

Babcock adds: "If they let her be executed, then what it tells us is that the death penalty in this country is just a joke. It's not for the worst of the worst. It is for the people who receive the worst legal representation and who are the most damaged and vulnerable."

Last year, Tennessee's Supreme Court ruled Pike had not shown circumstances that would justify commuting her sentence. Her appeals process had been exhausted and a date was set for her execution.

A federal appeals court had earlier ruled that the jury had already heard about her difficult childhood during testimony from her mother, father, and aunt during her trial. And that new evidence of bipolar disorder, PTSD, and brain damage "mostly repeated" what the jury had heard and would not have changed the verdict.

The row has some parallels with the high-profile case of murderer Lisa Montgomery, whose lawyers also argued she was a mentally ill victim of abuse who deserved mercy.

Montgomery's legal challenges failed to commute her sentence, and she was executed by lethal injection in Indiana in 2021 .

Unless she is granted clemency by Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, Pike will be executed on 30 September. That decision is unlikely to come until the last moment, and Lee has never granted clemency in a death penalty case before.

The Tennessee Supreme Court this week denied Pike's request to halt the execution. Her counsel say they have been discussing next steps.

On her execution day, Pike has requested an all-female team. She says being held down by a group of men will exacerbate her trauma. The state of Tennessee has said the goal is that female guards will transfer Pike to the prison where she will be executed but hasn't guaranteed it.

Colleen's mother May Martinez supports Christa's execution.

"She did the crime. I think she should pay for it," she said on Knoxville TV station WBIR in 2021, and told the BBC this week she still stands by those comments.

Pike should suffer before she dies, Martinez told WBIR. "I would feel better that she felt the same pain that Colleen did."

"My heart breaks every single day because I keep reliving it and reliving it, and I can't no more, and I want this to happen before I die," she added.

"There's not a day goes by that I don't think about Colleen or how she died and how rough it was. I just want Christa down so I can end it, relieve my daughter, so she finally can be resting."

The Justice Coalition, a victims' rights advocacy group, has raised money to help Martinez travel to Tennessee to watch the execution.

The group's executive director, Robert Bracewell, said this sentence was determined by a jury of Pike's peers and it is what Colleen's family want.

"We stand firm with the family that on the 30 September her execution ought to proceed."

Ashlee Sellars grapples with two seemingly conflicting beliefs: that Colleen's mother has a right to feel justice has been served and that everyone, including her friend Christa, deserves a chance at redemption.

"When I think about reconciling who you see on TV or the horrible tragedy that happened with Colleen, the only thing that makes sense to me is around mental health and trauma and the way that people process stuff in a moment when they don't have the things that they need," Sellars says.

"These horrible things happen in your youth and then those traumas moved through you, in our community, and you cause harm to somebody else."

Sellars met Pike in prison while serving a 25-year sentence for her involvement in a robbery-murder. They spoke to each other through the meal flaps in their doors on the high security unit. Now, Sellars works as an advocate for justice reform and victims of crime.

"People want to know that everyone's life matters, right? They want to know that Colleen's life mattered," she says.

"Christa in this moment, I think she is fighting much more for her life to matter than she is to actually live."

articles.title: Pope Leo draws staggering 800,000 faithful to heart of Paris for massive outdoor Mass
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV drew an estimated 800,000 to Place de la Concorde for a historic open-air Mass, urging French Catholics to share their faith openly.
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV drew an estimated 800,000 people into the heart of Paris on Saturday for a massive open-air Mass, filling one of the French republic’s most storied public squares as he urged Catholics to openly share their faith in an "increasingly secularized society." Flag-waving crowds packed the Champs-Élysées and Place de la Concorde as the American pope traveled roughly 1.2 miles through central Paris in the popemobile before celebrating Mass. The Vatican estimated attendance at 800,000, roughly 200,000 more people than had registered in advance. People of faith gathered in the streets, with families lifting babies and young children toward the popemobile as Leo made his way through the French capital. POPE LEO XIV RECEIVES 'SYMBOLIC’ SPHERE IN CHARITY'S PUSH FOR AI TO 'PROTECT HUMAN DIGNITY' "Seeing you gathered here," Leo told worshippers, he was looking upon the "heirs of France’s long and beautiful history of faith," according to Vatican News. The pope called on French Catholics not to keep that rich inheritance to themselves. FROM DISNEY MAGIC TO ANCIENT FAITH: DAVID HENRIE ON WHY GEN Z IS FLOCKING TO CHURCH "Let it overflow, so that those you meet may be refreshed and their thirst satisfied," Leo said. "From this beautiful city of Paris, I pray fervently that the living water of the Holy Spirit may flow throughout France." The setting carried particular resonance in a country known for its strict tradition of secularism. AMERICAN BISHOP ROBERT BARRON CALLS OUT ST. PAUL'S CATHEDRAL IN UK OVER NIGHTCLUB PARTNERSHIP It is notable that the Place de la Concorde was an execution ground during the French Revolution, where devoutly Catholic King Louis XVI and Queen Marie Antoinette were guillotined. Today, the square is closely associated with the French republic and regularly hosts Bastille Day celebrations. The decision to celebrate a papal Mass there drew criticism from supporters of France’s strict separation of church and state, who argued another site would have been more appropriate. The images also offered a striking contrast with another massive Paris spectacle just two years earlier. The 2024 Summer Olympics opening ceremony drew worldwide controversy over a tableau featuring drag performers that Christian leaders and other critics said mocked Christianity. POLL FINDS SHARP RISE IN YOUNG MEN CALLING RELIGION 'VERY IMPORTANT' The French Bishops’ Conference said at the time that the ceremony "included scenes of mockery and derision of Christianity," adding that Christians around the world had been "hurt by the outrageousness and provocation of certain scenes." The tableau was widely interpreted by critics as a parody of Leonardo da Vinci’s "The Last Supper," though Olympics organizers disputed that interpretation. Leo’s visit comes as France experiences a notable increase in adult conversions even as the country continues a decades-long decline in overall Catholic participation. Annual adult baptisms in France have tripled since 2016, reaching 13,000 this year, according to The Associated Press. Overall baptisms, however, have fallen sharply over the longer term, from 513,000 in 1980 to 186,000 in 2024. YOUNG MEN ARE RETURNING TO CHURCH — AND IT COULD RESHAPE AMERICA’S FUTURE Leo thanked French families, young people, catechumens and new Christians for bearing witness to their faith in what he described as an "increasingly secularized society," according to Vatican News. The scale of the pope’s reception was already apparent the night before the Mass as some 80,000 young people packed France’s national stadium Friday for a vigil featuring fireworks and a theatrical retelling of the country’s Catholic history. "Thank you for your courage! Thank you for your presence," Leo told them in French. "Thank you for your faith. You are the saints of France!" At Saturday’s Mass, Leo invoked France’s Catholic heritage and drew on the biblical image of "living water," telling worshippers that Jesus Christ could satisfy humanity’s desire for "life, truth, unity, peace, communion, and happiness." He also invoked French Catholic saints including Irenaeus, Martin and Francis de Sales while praising those who continue to work for "life, the family, truth, peace, fraternity and justice." The sea of people rivaled some of the largest public celebrations to fill the Champs-Élysées in recent decades, including France’s World Cup victories in 1998 and 2018, according to the AP. Leo’s four-day trip to France began Friday with a visit to the restored Notre Dame Cathedral, the first by a pope since the devastating 2019 fire. articles.title: Four American tourists among 6 killed in suspected gas leak blast in Athens
articles.summary: Two women reportedly injured after building collapse in Athens’ historic Plaka district.
articles.body:
Rescue teams have recovered the bodies of six people killed in a building collapse following a a blast in the historic centre of Athens, Greece, according to local authorities.

Documents and belongings found with four of the victims – two men and two women – on Saturday indicated they were United States citizens, Greek state broadcaster ERT and other local media reported.

The other two victims were reportedly an elderly couple, a British man and a Greek woman, who lived on the building’s second floor.

Two women were injured in an adjacent building, according to the fire department.

The blast that brought down the small, two-storey building in the popular tourist district of Plaka on Friday was believed to have been caused by a major gas leak, Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said. Neighbouring buildings were damaged and evacuated, he said.

“The damage extends to the entire street as well as the street behind [the building],” Doukas said. “We are talking about an unimaginable catastrophe.”

Two adjoining buildings severely damaged might have to be demolished, he said.

The Greek daily newspaper Kathimerini reported on Friday that the four tourists, who were due to leave their accommodation at about 11:00am (08:00 GMT), failed to board their flight back to the US.

A group of Plaka residents had alerted the municipality and the managers of the electricity and gas networks about the risks of short circuits or gas leaks in the area a year ago.

In a letter published by Kathimerini, the group called for the organisation of a security exercise to identify any potential shortcomings in the emergency response system.

The citizen movement “We Remain Active” also stated on social media that a resident of the street where the explosion occurred had reported a smell of gas for several weeks and had warned the authorities.

A Greek police spokeswoman confirmed on ERT that residents had made the report. However, the nature of the substance and its origin have not yet been determined.

Plaka lies at the foot of the Acropolis, Greece’s most visited ancient monument.

articles.title: China’s latest panda diplomats Ping Ping and Fu Shuang take flight as they head for Atlanta
articles.summary: Two giant pandas have left China on a flight bound for their new home at a zoo in Atlanta, where they will live on loan from the Chinese government, the latest episode in Beijing’s long tradition of using “panda diplomacy” to strengthen ties with other countries.
articles.body: Two giant pandas have left China on a flight bound for their new home at a zoo in Atlanta, where they will live on loan from the Chinese government, the latest episode in Beijing’s long tradition of using “panda diplomacy” to strengthen ties with other countries. They departed Chengdu, in southwestern China, at 2:55 a.m. Sunday morning local time, China’s state news agency Xinhua said. The flight came just a day after Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington concluded. During that visit, which was intended to address rising tensions between the world’s two superpowers, Xi and US President Donald Trump extended a trade truce and agreed to establish an AI hotline between the two countries. The Chengdu Giant Panda Breeding Research Base held a farewell ceremony for the two pandas and China formulated a “detailed transportation plan” to transport them to the US, which included packing fresh bamboo shoots and apples for them to eat during the flight, Xinhua reported. China also arranged for several veterinarians and breeders to remain at the zoo in Atlanta as the pandas enter quarantine upon arrival, the Xinhua added. The team at Zoo Atlanta and the Chinese team held “many online and offline meetings to carry out in-depth exchanges on the upgrading and transformation plan” for the venue that houses the pandas, according to Xinhua. “After the transformation, the activity space of the indoor exhibition area has been significantly expanded, and abundant facilities such as habitats, stone platforms and pools have been added, providing giant pandas with richer options for exploration and rest, Xinhua reported. Loaning pandas has long been a tool of Chinese diplomacy. “The giant panda has been an envoy of friendship between the Chinese and Americans,” Xi said on Thursday, referencing the half-century in which pandas lived in US zoos on loan from the Chinese government. That tradition was started by Chairman Mao Zedong in 1972, shortly after Richard Nixon became the first US president to visit China following the Communist Party’s rise to power in 1949. One of the pandas bound for Atlanta even shares the same name – Ping Ping, meaning peace – as the first ever panda Mao gifted to the Soviet Union in 1957. He was born on March 17, 2020, has large black patches around his eyes and is especially good at climbing trees, according to China’s National Forestry and Grassland Administration. The other panda, Fu Shuang, meaning double blessings, was born seven months later on October 18. She has a small tuft of fur on the top of her head, a slightly protruding forehead and finds food very easily, the administration said. Zookeepers at the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding selected the pair after considering their age, health, genetics and personality. “They should be docile and like each other, and hopefully be able to mate naturally,” the park’s deputy director Li Mingxi told Chinese state broadcaster CCTV. They are scheduled to arrive in Atlanta early on Sunday morning. The zoo has hosted several pandas before. Another pair, Lun Lun and Yang Yang, had seven offspring there between 2006 and 2016 before returning to Chengdu. Their destination – Zoo Atlanta – earlier in the year said they would be “delighted and honored” to welcome the two pandas. A banner displayed at the zoo on Saturday read “The future home of Ping Ping and Fu Shuang.” A Zoo Atlanta representative said the facility would not share information about Ping Ping and Fu Shuang’s planned arrival date and declined to comment further. China and the Atlanta zoo “will carry out in-depth academic and cultural exchanges to continuously enhance mutual understanding and friendship between the people of China and the United States,” Xinhua said. Panda diplomacy has offered some relief from the tensions increasingly shaping the US-China relationship in recent years, as the two countries compete in an AI arms race and engage in a spiraling trade war. Two giant pandas arrived in San Diego in June 2024, the first time China allowed new pandas to travel to the US in more than two decades, before a second pair travelled to Washington’s National Zoo later that year. In preparation for the move, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang have been quarantined for a month with a roster of live-in carers, Li said. The pandas have been trained for their long flight too, becoming used to their crate and loud noises. CNN’s Xiaoqian Lin, Farida Elsebai, Rebekah Riess, Mike Valerio and Mitchell McCluskey contributed reporting. This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title: A South African couple built a 305-sq-m luxury home using nearly 97 tonnes of reclaimed waste, including 55,636 kg of plastic
articles.summary: What if a luxury home could be built from material that would otherwise have gone to landfill?
articles.body: What if a luxury home could be built from material that would otherwise have gone to landfill? In Riebeek-Kasteel, a small town in South Africa's Western Cape, Louis Jansen van Vuuren and Hardy Olivier have turned that idea into their home, EcoSpace. According to Zerocrete, the 305-square-metre, double-storey residence is the world’s first luxury home built entirely with its Zerocrete material, which incorporates reclaimed plastic, fabric and glass waste. Zerocrete says construction diverted nearly 97 tonnes of non-recyclable waste from landfill, including 55,636 kilograms of reclaimed plastic, 26,115 kilograms of fabric and textiles, and 15,281 kilograms of glass. The company says the plastic is equivalent to nearly 4 million PET water bottles and forms the core of the home's walls and furniture. The project was developed as a proof of concept to show how waste-derived materials could be incorporated into a high-end residential building without abandoning conventional ideas of comfort or design.Fabric and glass round out the home's unusual material mixPlastic is only part of the material story. Zerocrete says EcoSpace incorporates 26,115 kilograms of discarded fabric and textiles, a quantity it equates to more than 186,000 T-shirts, into building materials valued for their insulation properties. Another 15,281 kilograms of reclaimed glass, which the company compares with more than 38,000 wine bottles, were incorporated into countertops and other surfaces. Zerocrete also says that 50% of the cement required for the project was replaced with a low-carbon alternative, which the company estimates prevented 283,000 kilograms of carbon dioxide emissions. That figure is a company-reported estimate rather than an independently verified measurement. Zerocrete says the project also created 36 new jobs and provided local artisans with training in working with the new material. The company's description of the house emphasises that the recycled content was not intended to remain hidden: coloured glass is visible in countertops, fibres contribute texture to walls and polished plastic gives some floors a terrazzo-like appearance.The couple brought decades of experience to the projectEcoSpace is not the couple's first experience creating distinctive homes. In an article published by Your Luxury Africa titled “EcoSpace: An Extraordinary Home Built from Waste”, Jansen van Vuuren and Olivier said they had owned five homes in France over 27 years, ranging from a small house in Lapeyrouse to a château in the French countryside. They eventually returned to South Africa and chose Riebeek-Kasteel for their new home. The couple said they were drawn to the town's location at the foot of the Kasteelberg, with a valley surrounded by vineyards and olive groves and views towards the Groot Winterberge mountains. They also described the town as having two distinct rhythms, becoming lively with visitors during weekends and holidays before returning to the quieter atmosphere of a rural village during the week. Their experience with historic and artistic properties also influenced the way EcoSpace was conceived, with the finished home combining the industrial appearance of Zerocrete surfaces with antique French pieces, contemporary furniture, art and Aubusson tapestries.The home's plastic came from a major South African retailerStructural engineer Johan Coetzee and his company were responsible for taking the project from concept through construction. In an article published by the Sunday Times titled “Stylish home of the future built from waste”, Coetzee said approximately 55 tonnes of non-recyclable plastic used in the building came from South African retailer Shoprite. The newspaper reported that the material was equivalent to about 3.9 million plastic bottles, broadly consistent with Zerocrete's more precise figure of 55,636 kilograms and its estimate of nearly 4 million PET bottles. Coetzee described the project as a prototype intended to demonstrate what could be achieved using waste-derived construction materials and said the construction cost remained aligned with standard market rates for a comparable home. The Sunday Times also reported Coetzee's estimate that the completed building produced less than 200 kilograms of carbon dioxide emissions per square metre, compared with an estimated 850 kilograms per square metre for conventional construction in South Africa. Those figures are Coetzee's stated estimates and should not be treated as an independently verified life-cycle assessment.The finished home keeps the focus on comfort and designAlthough developed as a proof of concept, EcoSpace was designed as a complete residential property, with bedrooms, bathrooms, living spaces, a studio and a garage. Zerocrete describes the 305-square-metre house as a double-storey property with a large open-plan ground floor connecting the lounge, dining and entertainment areas. The home has two en-suite bedrooms, including a main suite with a full bathroom containing both a bath and shower, while the guest bedroom has its own shower room. Upstairs, an office or studio has a further en-suite bathroom, bringing the total to 3.5 bathrooms, alongside a spacious garage. The material itself remains visible throughout the interiors, with coloured glass embedded in countertops, fibres adding texture to walls and polished plastics creating depth in the floors. Rather than attempting to disguise the origin of the materials, the design makes that history part of the aesthetic. The result is a house intended to demonstrate Zerocrete's central proposition: that industrial waste can be transformed into structural and decorative materials for a contemporary home without making sustainability the only defining feature of the finished space.You use AI every day. articles.title: FTC: Make AI developers liable for agents' conduct
articles.summary: US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) chairman Andrew Ferguson said on Friday he would resist describing AI agents as autonomous actors that \"break loose\"
articles.body: US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) chairman Andrew Ferguson said on Friday he would resist describing AI agents as autonomous actors that "break loose" with "wills and desires of their own," suggesting the developers who instruct agents would be the ones liable for harm."I'm going to continue as long as I am chairman to resist this anthropomorphizing of these tools," Ferguson said at the Reuters Momentum AI Austin event. "If someone tells a tool to do something, and the tool does it, I don't think we would say, 'Oh, what do we do about the tool?'"Ferguson's remarks illustrated potential avenues for the Trump administration to take as incidents rise in which agentic AI testing resulted in unauthorised access to corporate or govt data.Artificial intelligence companies have sometimes described systems as acting beyond human control, but subsequent reviews of audit trails have shown that the systems were carrying out instructions they had been given, Ferguson said.Recent incidents involving AI agents accessing external systems have prompted govts and industry leaders to examine whether existing oversight and cybersecurity measures are sufficient.The US should utilise existing legal tools, Ferguson said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Clavicular case explained: Experts reveal how livestreams and social media may affect the trial
articles.summary: Controversial influencer Clavicular, whose real name is Braden Peters, is facing serious criminal allegations in Massachusetts, including rape and
articles.body: Controversial influencer Clavicular, whose real name is Braden Peters, is facing serious criminal allegations in Massachusetts, including rape and drugging someone for sexual intercourse. The 20-year-old creator has not been taken into custody and is scheduled to appear in court on October 14. As prosecutors prepare their case, legal expert Seth Zuckerman has explained how Peters’ livestreams, social media posts and material he has publicly shared could become important evidence.Clavicular rape charge and the role of social mediaThe allegations centre on an incident that police say occurred on May 23, 2025, at Peters’ family home in Chatham, Massachusetts. According to the criminal complaint, the alleged victim was 17 at the time.Investigators reportedly reviewed livestream footage connected to the incident. The complaint says the teenager allegedly felt “peer-pressured” to drink and that Peters knew her age. The case includes charges of rape, drugging someone for sexual intercourse and procuring liquor for someone under 21.Seth Zuckerman, a former New York City prosecutor and celebrity criminal defence attorney, said prosecutors could rely heavily on available footage.“The prosecutors will use any and all videos that corroborate their allegations,” Zuckerman tells PEOPLE of the case.He also explained that other material could potentially become relevant if prosecutors argue it shows a pattern or supports their version of events.“They will also use these videos if they constitute prior bad acts for which he cannot be charged but which help demonstrate their theory,” Zuckerman adds.The charges remain allegations, and Peters has not been convicted in the case.Clavicular’s posts could create legal risksPeters has publicly discussed the controversy through his social media accounts. He has shared videos that appear connected to the alleged livestream, along with messages exchanged with the woman identified by other reports as the alleged victim.Zuckerman said Peters’ decision to publicly release material could have consequences beyond public opinion.“He is releasing evidence that he believes tends to disprove the allegations as a public relations ploy,” Zuckerman explains to PEOPLE. “Any statement he makes about the allegations can be used against him in any proceeding, including the criminal case.”The case also overlaps with a civil lawsuit filed earlier by influencer Aleksandra Vasilevna Mendoza, known online as Alorah Ziva. Peters has denied her allegations through his attorney.According to Zuckerman, the civil proceedings could affect the criminal case because statements made during the lawsuit may become relevant. His lawyers could seek to pause that case while the criminal proceedings continue.Peters has also faced unrelated legal matters, including a Florida firearm case that ended with a no-contest plea and probation. Zuckerman noted that whether prior incidents can be introduced at trial will ultimately depend on a judge’s ruling.If convicted of the top charge, Peters could face up to 20 years in prison. Zuckerman said a case of this complexity could take 12 to 18 months or longer to reach a verdict.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
